resources.string: The app could not apply that backup. Your settings did not change.
The app writes a backup on a timer.
Fill in the connection details first.
The app deletes the oldest backup when there are more than this. It always keeps the newest one. Each device counts only its own backups.
Wait for a connection that costs you nothing

A backup can be a few megabytes, and it goes out every time the timer comes round. With this on, the app waits for Wi-Fi, or for any other connection that Android does not count as metered. With it off, a backup goes out over mobile data as soon as it is due. Folder locations need no connection at all, so this setting only shows when a backup goes to a server or a cloud account. This setting is on by default.
Wait until your device is plugged in

This is what the app always did. Turn it off if you rarely charge your device for long enough, because a backup that never finds a charger never runs, and nothing tells you that it did not. The work itself is a few seconds of copying, so it costs little battery.
The app encrypts each backup. You need the passphrase to restore one.

The app stores the passphrase on this device, because an automatic backup has nobody to type it. This protects the backup file where it goes, for example in a cloud folder. It does not protect it from a person who holds your unlocked device. Write the passphrase down: without it, a backup cannot be restored.

This backup holds words that you typed, or text that you copied, and no passphrase protects it. The app writes it to your locations on a timer. Turn on a passphrase, or turn off the dictionary, the clipboard and the swipe style in What goes in a backup.
The app wrote %1$s. It left out %2$s, because the backup was too large.

The full address of the folder to write into, for example https://cloud.example.com/remote.php/dav/files/me/backups
If your server can make app passwords, use one here instead of your account password.
This address is not https. The app sends your user name and password with every upload, and on a plain http address anyone on the network can read them, so the app does not use it.
The app can write to its folder in your Drive.
The app needs your permission first.

The app writes to a hidden folder of its own in your Drive. It cannot see your other files, and the folder does not show up beside your documents. To take this permission back, go to your Google account and open the list of apps with account access. To keep backups you can see in the Drive app, select A folder you can see above.
Leave this empty for Amazon S3. For other services, put their address here, for example https://your-account.r2.cloudflarestorage.com or the address of your own MinIO server.
Use us-east-1 if your service does not have regions.
Leave this empty to put backups at the top of the bucket.
Put the bucket in the path
Turn this on for MinIO, and for any address that is an IP address. Leave it off for Amazon S3 and Cloudflare R2.
This endpoint is not https. The app signs every request with your secret key, and on a plain http address anyone on the network can read what is sent.
Leave this empty to use the directory you land in after you sign in.
Encrypts the connection before the app signs in. Leave this on unless your server cannot do it.
Without TLS, your password and your backup both cross the network as plain text that anyone in between can read. If you must leave this off, turn on Protect with a passphrase in Automatic backup.
The app could not finish signing in. Try again.
The app could not open a browser to sign in.

The app gets a folder of its own inside your Dropbox and can see nothing else. You can find the folder under Apps, and you can delete it. To take this permission back, open the connected apps list in your Dropbox account.
This device has not synced yet
Each automatic backup goes to the locations that you tick in Automatic backup. Sync uses the locations that you tick in Sync devices. Nothing goes to a WM Keyboard server.

Automatic backups do not go here
Each automatic backup goes to every location that you tick here. A location that you untick keeps its settings, and gets no backups until you tick it again.
Add a location on the Backup & restore screen first.

Your devices must share at least one of these locations. If you tick more than one, the app writes the sync file to each of them, so sync keeps working while one service is down. That uses a little more data.
Tick a location in Back up to.
Tick a location in Sync through.
We strongly suggest that you turn on Protect with a passphrase in Automatic backup first
We strongly suggest that you turn on Protect with a passphrase first

No passphrase protects these files. Anyone who can open the location can read your API keys and passwords, and use them. We strongly suggest that you turn on Protect with a passphrase in Automatic backup first.
It works. Backups can go here.
One passphrase protects the automatic backups and the sync files. Use the same passphrase on every device that syncs.
Save a copy that you move yourself
Restore from a backup or a settings file
Keep your keyboard the same on all your devices
Share changes with your other devices
About a minute after you change something, and every hour for changes from other devices
At a fixed interval. Uses the least data.
Only when you press Sync now
Some settings stay on each device, because they only fit that device: the keyboard size and position, one-handed mode, the hardware keyboard, paired computers and the app lock.

Each device keeps one sync file at a location. Every device reads the files of the others, and the newest change to each setting wins. The first time a device syncs, the settings of your other devices win, and anything that only this device has goes to the others.
Another device uses a different passphrase. Use the same passphrase on every device.
